20-july-plot: Since 1938 groups within the German Army and the Military Intelligence Organization had plotted an overthrow. Early leaders included Major General Hans Oster, Colonel General Ludwig Beck and Field Marshal Erwin von Witzleben, who made contact with civilians such as Carl Goerdeler and Helmuth James von Moltke. Moltke opposed killing Hitler and wanted him put on trial. Most plotters were conservative nationalists, though the historian Judith Michel describes the wider circle as including liberal democrats, social democrats and even communists.

By mid-1943 the war was turning against Germany. Claus von Stauffenberg, severely wounded in North Africa in April 1943, concluded after Stalingrad that assassination was a lesser moral evil than Hitler's remaining in power. Olbricht proposed using the Replacement Army's Operation Valkyrie, a plan for civil breakdown, to mobilise the Reserve Army for a coup. At least five earlier attempts failed.

On 1 July 1944 Stauffenberg became Chief of Staff to General Friedrich Fromm in Berlin, which gave him access to Hitler's conferences. On 14 July he held back because Himmler was absent. On 20 July he flew to the Wolf's Lair with a bomb in his briefcase. It appears to have been moved unwittingly behind a table leg by Heinz Brandt. Hitler suffered singed trousers, a perforated eardrum and conjunctivitis.

Believing Hitler dead, Stauffenberg bluffed through three checkpoints with his aide Werner von Haeften and was airborne by 13:00. Hours after the blast, Wehrmacht units were ordered to seize several cities. At about 18:10 General Joachim von Kortzfleisch refused Olbricht's orders in Berlin, shouting that the Führer was alive, and was arrested. General Fritz Lindemann, who held the only copy of the radio proclamation, did not appear. Within hours the regime reasserted control.

Himmler's Gestapo, driven by a furious Hitler, rounded up nearly everyone with the remotest connection to the plot. Letters and diaries revealed the plots of 1938, 1939 and 1943 and led to further arrests, including Colonel General Franz Halder, and under the Sippenhaft laws many relatives were arrested. The planned government, with Beck as provisional head of state and Goerdeler as chancellor, never took office. A 1951 survey found that only a third of respondents viewed the plotters positively. At the first memorial service, in 1954, President Theodor Heuss said that refusals to carry out orders had achieved historic greatness.
2000-summer-olympics: Sydney won the right to host the Games on 24 September 1993, at the 101st IOC Session in Monte Carlo, Monaco. It was selected over Beijing, Berlin, Istanbul and Manchester in four rounds of voting. Brasília, Milan and Tashkent made bids but withdrew during the bidding process. The Games were the first to feature at least 300 events in the official sports program, and the final Games under the IOC presidency of Juan Antonio Samaranch, who was succeeded by Jacques Rogge.

Several quasi-government bodies built and ran the Games, among them the Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games (SOCOG), the Olympic Coordination Authority, which oversaw construction, and the Olympic Roads and Transport Authority. IBM provided technology and Telstra telecommunications. The Olympic torch relay began in Greece and travelled to Australia through a number of Oceania island nations. The organisers treated the project in phases, from positioning in 1993 to 1996 to implementation in 2000 and wind-down in 2001.

A cycle of four arts festivals led up to the Games, beginning with the Festival of the Dreaming in 1997, founded by the artistic director Rhoda Roberts, who later co-directed segments of the Opening Ceremony. The emblem, nicknamed the Millennium Man, was designed by FHA Image Design and showed a stylised torch-bearer with limbs like boomerangs. The official mascots were Syd the platypus, Millie the echidna and Olly the kookaburra. In all, 750 gold, 750 silver and 780 bronze medals were minted, the bronze ones from withdrawn Australian one-cent and two-cent coins.

Teams from 199 countries took part. The United States led the final medal tally, followed by Russia and China, with Australia fourth. Cameroon, Colombia, Latvia, Mozambique and Slovenia won a gold medal for the first time, and Barbados, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Macedonia, Saudi Arabia and Vietnam won their first Olympic medals. The IOC awarded Sydney the Pierre de Coubertin Trophy for the collaboration and happiness shown by its people.

In 2000 the Auditor-General of New South Wales reported that the Games cost A$6.6 billion, with a net cost to the public between A$1.7 and A$2.4 billion, and funds were shifted from education and health programs in the years before. Press reports praised the organisation, and Lord Coe later called the Games a benchmark when London prepared for 2012.
2004-indian-ocean-earthquake-and-tsunami: The earthquake struck at 07:58:53 local time on 26 December 2004, off the west coast of Aceh. It was caused by a rupture along the boundary between the Burma plate and the Indian plate, where the Indian plate slides under the overriding Burma plate. The slip took place in two phases over several minutes: it began off Aceh and moved north-west, paused for about 100 seconds, then continued north towards the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, more slowly. Its estimated magnitude was first given as 8.8 and later revised upward.
No tsunami warning system existed in the Indian Ocean. Tsunamis there are rarer than in the Pacific, and the last major one had followed the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883.

The sudden rise of the seabed displaced vast volumes of water. In Aceh the waves came about 20 minutes after the quake. Survivors described the sea withdrawing from the port of Ulèë Lheuë, exposing the seabed, before two steep black waves moved into Banda Aceh as a turbulent bore full of debris. Sri Lanka, about 1,700 km away, was struck around two hours after the earthquake, with approximately 35,000 killed, and Thailand about two hours after, where around 8,000 died, many of them tourists at resorts such as Khao Lak.

The waves also reached the Indian states of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh, and the Maldives, whose reefs and deep channels between atolls reduced the damage. They travelled 5,000 km west to Somalia, where about 289 people died, and killed people as far away as Kenya, Tanzania, Seychelles and South Africa.

The Tsunami Evaluation Coalition's final report counted 227,898 dead, while the United Nations Office of the Special Envoy for Tsunami Recovery gives 229,866. Most estimates for Indonesia are around 170,000. The report warned that data on the missing in particular are subject to error. Salt water contaminated wells, aquifers and farmland, and mangroves, coral reefs and coastal wetlands were damaged.

Aid agencies feared epidemics of cholera, typhoid and other diseases and worked to provide sanitation and drinking water; the death toll from disease was kept down by the quick response. The World Food Programme fed more than 1.3 million people. Donations to the response totalled more than US$14 billion.
2004-summer-olympics: Athens had lost its bid for the 1996 Summer Olympics to Atlanta on 18 September 1990. Under the direction of Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki it bid again, and the 106th IOC Session in Lausanne chose it on 5 September 1997. The bid drew on the history of the Games and was praised for its low scale, humility and focused message, unlike the 1996 bid, which had been seen as arrogant.

The Greek government spent close to 9 billion euros on the Games. The Athens 2004 Organizing Committee (ATHOC) finished its work as a company in 2005 with a surplus of 130.6 million euros. The Games brought a new airport, an expanded metro, a tram, a suburban railway and the Attiki Odos ring motorway.

The flame was lit at Ancient Olympia on 25 March 2004 and, for the first time, travelled around the world to past and future host cities before returning to Greece. The opening ceremony, directed by the choreographer Dimitris Papaioannou, took place on 13 August and the Games ran until 29 August.

In all 10,625 athletes, about 600 more than expected, took part with 5,501 team officials from 201 countries, in 301 medal events in 28 sports. It was the first time since 1996 that every country with a National Olympic Committee attended. The marathon started in the town of Marathon and finished in the Panathenaic Stadium, and the shot put was held in the stadium at Olympia.

Athens became the fourth city to host the Summer Games twice, with Paris, London and Los Angeles. The United States led the final medal table, followed by China and Russia, and Greece came 15th. Chile, Chinese Taipei, the Dominican Republic, Georgia and Israel won their first Olympic gold medals. The new medal obverse, designed by Elena Votsi, showed the Panathenaic Stadium, replacing a design that had depicted the Roman Colosseum.

The cost of the Games and a possible contribution to the Greek government-debt crisis of 2010–18 has been debated, mostly in popular media, though there is little or no evidence for the claim. A cost-benefit evaluation presented to the Greek Parliament in January 2013 found the net economic benefit for Greece positive.
2008-financial-crisis: In the 1990s the U.S. Congress passed legislation to expand affordable housing through looser financing laws, and in 1999 parts of the Glass–Steagall Act of 1933 were repealed, so that institutions could mix commercial banking and insurance with investment banking and proprietary trading. From 2000 to 2003 the Federal Reserve lowered the federal funds rate target from 6.5 per cent to 1.0 per cent to soften the effects of the dot-com collapse and the September 11 attacks.

Between 1998 and 2006 the price of the typical American house rose by 124 per cent, and the ratio of the median home price to median household income rose from about 3 in the 1980s and 1990s to 4.6 in 2006. Lenders lowered their standards. By 2005 many dropped the required FICO score for prime loans from 660 to 620, and loans moved from full documentation to none, including the so-called NINJA mortgages.

As interest rates rose from 2004 to 2006, payments on adjustable-rate mortgages spiked and defaults followed. New Century filed for bankruptcy protection on 2 April 2007, and on 14 September 2007 Northern Rock received support from the Bank of England and a bank run followed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average reached its peak close of 14,164.53 on 9 October 2007.

On 7 September 2008 the federal government took over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. On 15 September Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy after the Federal Reserve declined to guarantee its loans, and the Dow fell 504.48 points, or 4.42 per cent. The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act and the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program became law on 3 October 2008.

The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, a $787 billion stimulus, was approved on 13 February 2009, and the Dow closed at a six-year low on 20 February amid fears that the largest banks would have to be nationalised. Assessments vary, but suggest that about 8.7 million American jobs were lost, with unemployment rising from 5 per cent in 2007 to 10 per cent in October 2009. The Dodd–Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act was passed in 2010 and weakened by a law of 2018, and countries adopted the Basel III capital and liquidity standards.
2008-summer-olympics: Beijing was elected host city on 13 July 2001, during the 112th IOC Session in Moscow. After two rounds of voting it defeated bids from Toronto, Paris, Istanbul and Osaka, with a majority in the second round that made further voting unnecessary. The Chinese government promoted the Games actively and invested heavily in new sports venues and transport. Of the 37 venues used, twelve were built specially.

Football was played in Qinhuangdao, Shanghai, Shenyang and Tianjin, and sailing in Qingdao. Because of the uncertainties of equine diseases, the equestrian events were held in Hong Kong. Beijing also added seven subway lines and a new airport terminal designed by Norman Foster, and some stadiums were built on the former site of hutong neighbourhoods.

The torch relay, on the theme Journey of Harmony, lasted 130 days and covered 137,000 kilometres, the longest distance of any Olympic torch relay since the tradition began in 1936. It met protests by pro-Tibet supporters along its route, and the IOC afterwards barred future organisers from staging international torch relays.

The Games ran from 8 to 24 August 2008, and 10,942 athletes from 204 National Olympic Committees competed in 28 sports and 302 events. The opening ceremony began at 8:00 pm on 8 August in the Beijing National Stadium, known as the Bird's Nest, a time chosen because the number eight is associated with prosperity in Chinese culture. It was co-directed by Zhang Yimou and had a cast of over 15,000, and leaders from 105 countries and territories attended.

The Marshall Islands, Montenegro and Tuvalu competed for the first time. A total of 125 Olympic records, 37 of them world records, were set; in swimming, 25 world records fell, in suits such as the LZR Racer. China won the most gold medals, 48, and 100 medals in all, while the United States won the most medals overall, 112, and Russia placed third. In the closing ceremony on 24 August the Olympic flag was handed to London.

It was the first time China had hosted the Olympic Games and the third time the Summer Games had been held in East Asia, after Tokyo in 1964 and Seoul in 1988. A record 87 countries won at least one medal, and 54 of them won gold. Concerns raised before and during the Games included claims that China had broken its pledge of open media access, human rights, air pollution and protests over Tibet.

An IOC investigation cleared members of the Chinese women's gymnastics team who were accused of being too young to compete. Many of the worst fears did not materialise: the world's media generally accepted the Games as a logistical success, and favourable weather meant that the air quality was not as bad as feared.
2010-haiti-earthquake: The island of Hispaniola, shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic, is seismically active. An earthquake on 7 May 1842 destroyed Cap-Haïtien and the Sans-Souci Palace, and one of magnitude 8.0 struck the Dominican Republic on 4 August 1946 and produced a tsunami that killed 1,790 people. Construction standards in Haiti were low and the country had no building codes. Buildings were often raised wherever they could fit, some on slopes with insufficient foundations, and a representative of Catholic Relief Services estimated that about two million Haitians lived as squatters on land they did not own.

The earthquake struck at 16:53 local time on 12 January 2010, at a depth of 13 kilometres, on blind thrust faults associated with the Enriquillo-Plantain Garden fault system, and lasted less than 30 seconds. Shaking reached intensity IX on the Modified Mercalli scale in Port-au-Prince and its suburbs, and was more severe than for other quakes of similar magnitude because of the shallow depth. The strongest aftershock, of magnitude 5.9, came on 20 January and collapsed seven buildings in Petit-Goâve.

A localised tsunami, probably from an underwater landslide, hit the beach at Petit Paradis, and at least three people were swept out to sea. Prime Minister Jean-Max Bellerive estimated that 250,000 residences and 30,000 commercial buildings needed to be demolished. The main prison in Port-au-Prince was destroyed, allowing around 4,000 inmates to escape, and President René Préval escaped unhurt from the National Palace. More than 1,300 schools and 50 health care facilities were destroyed.

The Dominican Republic was the first country to send aid. Teams from many countries arrived, and a telethon, Hope for Haiti Now, aired on 22 January and raised US$58 million by the next day. The government handed control of the airport to the United States to ease flight operations, and there was confusion over who was in charge.

On 22 January the United Nations noted that the emergency phase was drawing to a close, and the Haitian government called off the search for survivors the next day. Estimates of the dead differ widely. The Haitian government reported 230,000 in mid-February 2010 and, on 12 January 2011, more than 316,000, while a Radio Netherlands investigation suggested about 92,000. Six months after the quake, as much as 98 per cent of the rubble remained uncleared and 1.6 million people lived in camps of tents and tarps.
2011-christchurch-earthquake: The earthquake struck at 12:51 p.m. local time on Tuesday 22 February 2011, centred 6.7 kilometres (4.2 mi) south-east of the central business district. Scientists classified it as an intraplate earthquake. GNS Science considers it part of the aftershock sequence of the magnitude 7.1 Canterbury earthquake of 4 September 2010, although a seismologist from Geoscience Australia treats it as a separate event because it lay on a separate fault system. Both quakes occurred on blind or unknown faults, though a 1991 report by New Zealand's Earthquake Commission had predicted moderate earthquakes in Canterbury, with liquefaction. Buildings and infrastructure were already weakened by the 2010 quake and its aftershocks.

The shaking lasted about 10 seconds, but the damage was severe because the focus was shallow and close to the city. Peak ground accelerations were the highest ever recorded in New Zealand, and the movement was mainly vertical, with eyewitnesses describing people being tossed into the air. Liquefaction in the eastern suburbs produced around 400,000 tonnes of silt. Many older buildings, especially those of unreinforced masonry or built before stringent codes, were damaged. Because the quake came at lunchtime, some people on the footpaths were buried by collapsed buildings. It killed 185 people from more than 20 countries, and over half of the deaths were in the six-storey Canterbury Television building, which collapsed and caught fire.

Eighty per cent of the city lost power at first. A local state of emergency was superseded on 23 February by a national one, only the second in New Zealand's history, which remained in force until 30 April. Search and rescue teams from New Zealand, Australia, the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan, Taiwan, China and Singapore worked in the city, and the New Zealand Defence Force carried out its largest operation on New Zealand soil. A Central City Red Zone was set up on the day of the quake.

The government set up a Royal Commission in March 2011 to examine the causes of building failure and the adequacy of building codes, and the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority was created on 29 March. About 10,000 houses were expected to need demolition and over 100,000 were damaged. Areas ruined by liquefaction and rockslides were placed in residential red zones, and through voluntary buyouts the Crown and insurers removed over 8,000 homes; the last demolition was completed in October 2021.

Christchurch could not host its Rugby World Cup matches in 2011, and the national census planned for 8 March was postponed to 2013. In the year to June 2011 the city's population fell by 8,900, and it took until 2017 to recover the loss. A national memorial service was held on 18 March at North Hagley Park.
2011-tohoku-earthquake-and-tsunami: The earthquake repeated the mechanism of the 869 Sanriku earthquake, estimated at a magnitude of at least 8.4, which also sent a large tsunami across the Sendai plain. Three tsunami deposits identified in the plain, all formed within the last 3,000 years, suggest a recurrence interval of 800 to 1,100 years for large tsunamigenic earthquakes. In 2007 the probability of an earthquake of magnitude 8.1–8.3 within thirty years was estimated at 99%. Seismologists had nonetheless expected the next great quake at the Sagami Trough, south-west of Tokyo, where the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake struck, and the Japan Trench had not been expected to produce quakes above magnitude 8.0.

The shock came at 14:46 JST on 11 March 2011 at a depth of 32 km and lasted about six minutes. The United States Geological Survey first reported it as 7.9, then raised it to 8.8, 8.9 and 9.0, and in 2016 to 9.1. Intensity 7, the highest on the Japan Meteorological Agency scale, was registered at Kurihara in Miyagi Prefecture. Parts of north-eastern Japan shifted as much as 2.4 metres towards North America, and a 400-kilometre stretch of coast dropped by 0.6 metres.

An upthrust of 6 to 8 metres along a seabed strip 180 km wide produced the tsunami, which flooded about 561 square kilometres of Japan. Residents of Sendai had only eight to ten minutes of warning, and more than a hundred evacuation sites were washed away. Snow fell minutes before or after the waves, depending on the place. The tsunami crossed the Pacific, and waves 2 metres high struck the coast of Chile.

Of the 19,759 deaths in the official figures, 10,567 were in Miyagi, 5,145 in Iwate and 3,920 in Fukushima. Drowning caused 90.64 per cent of them, and people over 60 made up 65.8 per cent. More than 340,000 people were displaced in the Tōhoku region.

At the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant the waves overtopped the seawalls and destroyed the diesel backup power, three reactors melted down and hydrogen explosions followed. Residents within 20 km were evacuated, and over 200,000 people in all. About 4.4 million households lost electricity, rolling blackouts began in the Tokyo area on 14 March, and the tsunami left an estimated 5 million tonnes of debris, some of which washed up in Canada and the United States. The government mobilised the Self-Defense Forces and many countries sent rescue teams.
2018-armenian-revolution: Demonstrations began in March 2018 when members of the Republican Party did not rule out nominating Serzh Sargsyan for prime minister, which would continue his rule, as president or prime minister, since March 2007. He had amended the constitution in 2015 to remove the term limits that would have prevented this. The Republican Party had been in power since 1999. Between 2012 and 2017 reported trust in the national government was 25 per cent. Nikol Pashinyan, a member of parliament and head of the Civil Contract party, led the protests, which Armenians know by the hashtag MerzhirSerzhin, meaning Reject Serzh. Pashinyan called it a Velvet Revolution.

On 31 March 2018 Pashinyan began a protest walk called Im Qayl, my step, from Gyumri through Vanadzor, Dilijan, Hrazdan and Abovyan, reaching Yerevan on 13 April. The Republican Party nominated Sargsyan, and on 17 April, when the vote was due, riot police stopped protesters trying to block the National Assembly. Sargsyan was elected prime minister, and the crowds reached 50,000 on the night of 21 April. On 22 April Pashinyan and Sargsyan met for three minutes, Sargsyan walked out and accused the opposition of blackmail, and police detained Pashinyan and hundreds of protesters.

Pashinyan was released on 23 April, and that afternoon Sargsyan resigned, saying that he had been wrong and Pashinyan right. On 25 April the Armenian Revolutionary Federation left the ruling coalition, and by 28 April the opposition parties in parliament had said they would back Pashinyan. On 1 May parliament voted on his candidacy, with 56 votes against and 45 for, the Republican Party opposing him. A nationwide strike and road blockade followed on 2 May, with about 150,000 people at an evening rally in Republic Square.

On 8 May 2018 parliament voted again, and Pashinyan, the only candidate, was elected prime minister with 59 votes to 42; all votes against came from the Republican Party. Commentators described the revolution as a shift in Armenia's domestic politics, with pro-Russian politicians ousted and a reformist government in their place, and as a chance to realign foreign policy toward Europe. It was also seen as contradicting the idea that post-Soviet leaders were irreplaceable. The event is compared by some to the peaceful revolutions in other post-Soviet states.
26-baku-commissars: The Baku Commune lasted from 13 April to 25 July 1918. It came to power after the bloody confrontation with the city's Muslim population known as the March Days, and, modelled on the Paris Commune, it had its own Council of People's Commissars and Commissariat of Foreign Affairs. It faced shortages of food and supplies and the threat of an Ottoman army, yet nationalised the oil industry. Its Cheka executed only two people, both members of the Soviet caught embezzling public funds.

After the Baku Red Army failed in an attack on Ganja, the Dashnaks, Right SRs and Mensheviks invited the British troops of General Dunsterville to defend the city. On 25 July the majority of the Soviet voted to call in the British, the Bolsheviks resigned, and the Centrocaspian Dictatorship took over.

The Bolshevik leaders tried to reach Astrakhan, but the Caspian fleet intercepted their ship and, after an hour's bombardment, forced them back to Baku, where most were imprisoned. During the fall of Baku to Ottoman forces in September they were freed, with Anastas Mikoyan among their rescuers, and boarded the ship Turkmen for Astrakhan. According to recent historians, the sailors chose Krasnovodsk instead for fear of arrest in Astrakhan. There the town's commandant arrested them and asked the Ashkhabad Committee of the Socialist Revolutionary Fyodor Funtikov for orders.

British Major-General Wilfrid Malleson suggested that the commissars be handed over as hostages, but his liaison officer, Captain Reginald Teague-Jones, did not pass on the request; the historian Richard H. Ullman held that he could have stopped the killings and chose not to. The executions took place between the stations of Pereval and Akhcha-Kuyma. Mikoyan survived, for reasons still uncertain.

Soviet officials blamed British agents, Britain denied any part, and the dispute soured relations between the two governments. Funtikov, who also put the blame on Teague-Jones, was tried and shot in Baku in 1926. The commissars, who were of many ethnicities, among them Greek, Latvian, Jewish, Russian, Georgian, Armenian and Azerbaijani, were reburied in 1920 in a central square in Baku and honoured in films, stamps, Isaak Brodsky's painting and Sergei Yesenin's Ballad of the Twenty-six. In 2009 Azerbaijani authorities demolished the 26 Commissars Memorial and reburied the remains at Hovsan Cemetery on 26 January.
2nd-king-edward-viis-own-gurkha-rifles: The Sirmoor Battalion was the first Gurkha unit in the service of the East India Company to see action, in the 3rd Mahratta War in 1817. As the 8th (Sirmoor) Local Battalion it won its first battle honour at Bhurtpore in 1825, and in the First Sikh War it fought at Bhudaiwal, Aliwal and Sobraon; when the Sikhs seized its colour, a small party of Gurkhas led by a havildar cut its way into their lines and took it back.

In the Indian Mutiny the battalion stayed loyal to Britain. For its part at Hindu Rao's House it received the Queen's Truncheon, which replaced the colours it gave up on becoming a rifle regiment in 1858. It became the 2nd Gurkha Regiment in 1861 and took the Prince of Wales as royal patron in 1876. In the First World War it served first in Flanders; the 2nd Battalion went on to Egypt, and the 1st to Persia and Mesopotamia, where it helped take Baghdad.

In the Second World War the 1st Battalion fought at El Alamein and Monte Cassino, the 2nd was captured in Malaya and spent much of the war as prisoners of the Japanese, and the 3rd took part in the Chindit operations in Burma in 1943. In the British Army after 1947 the regiment served in the Malayan Emergency from 1948 to 1960 and then in Malaya, Borneo, Brunei and Hong Kong, where its two battalions merged in 1992.

In 1947 the regiment's 4th Battalion passed to the Indian Army as the 5th Battalion, 8th Gurkha Rifles (Sirmoor Rifles), keeping the old title at the request of its first Indian commanding officer, Nisi Kanta Chatterji. It fought in the wars against Pakistan in 1965, at the Fatwal Ridge, and in 1971, in the defence of Chamb-Akhnur.

The 2nd Gurkhas were the only Gurkha regiment without a khukuri on the cap badge. Their red piping, adopted in 1858 from the British 60th Rifles through links forged at the Siege of Delhi, and the red toorie on the cap marked them out. Their Victoria Crosses include those of Subedar Lalbahadur Thapa in Tunisia in 1943 and Rifleman Bhanbhagta Gurung in Burma in 1945.
